content: Indian Ginseng, also known as Withania somnifera or Ashwagandha, has specific dosing recommendations based on its form and intended use. For capsules, the recommended dose is 1 to 6 grams of the whole herb taken orally once daily. In tea form, it is suggested to consume three cups daily, prepared using 1 to 6 grams of the whole herb. For tinctures, the recommended dose is 2 to 4 milliliters taken orally three times daily. Ashwagandha is classified as an adaptogen, meaning it helps the body adapt to internal and external stressors, combats fatigue, and enhances stamina. There is insufficient information available regarding certain effects and interactions of Ashwagandha. However, it is known to increase the effects of several medications through pharmacodynamic synergism, which may enhance central nervous system (CNS) depression. These medications include amobarbital, amphetamine, azelastine, brompheniramine, butabarbital, butalbital, carbinoxamine, chloral hydrate, chlorpheniramine, cinnarizine, clemastine, cyclizine, cyproheptadine, dexchlorpheniramine, dexmedetomidine, dextroamphetamine, dimenhydrinate, diphenhydramine, doxylamine, hydroxyzine, pentobarbital, phenobarbital, primidone, promethazine, triclophos, and triprolidine. The significance of these interactions is generally classified as minor or unknown, but caution is advised due to the potential for enhanced CNS depression. Regarding pregnancy and lactation, Ashwagandha is categorized as Pregnancy Category X, indicating that it is contraindicated during pregnancy due to potential risks to the fetus. There is no specific information available regarding its safety during lactation. However, in general, controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk for other substances in this category.
